extract.n: As a verb, extract is stressed on the second syllable (ik-STRACT), while the noun is stressed on the first (EK-stract), a classic pronunciation trap. It means to pull something out, whether physically, like a tooth, or by processing, like oil, minerals or juice. It also works for data and ideas: extract key points from a report. It is more formal and technical than take out or remove. Common partners are extract information, extract data and extract a confession. Extract from is the usual preposition.
x: The dentist had to extract two of his wisdom teeth last spring.
This software can extract text from scanned documents in seconds.
Police failed to extract a confession from the suspect.

intense.n: Intense describes something felt or experienced at a very high level: intense heat, intense pain, intense focus, intense competition. It is stronger than strong and more neutral than extreme. It can also describe a person who takes things very seriously, sometimes with a slightly negative feel. Do not confuse it with intensive, which describes effort concentrated into a short time, as in an intensive course. Stress the second syllable: in-TENSE. The adverb is intensely, and the noun is intensity.
x: The intense heat made it impossible to work outside after noon.
She felt intense relief when the results finally arrived.
Both teams have an intense rivalry that goes back decades.

expenditure.n: Expenditure is a formal noun for money spent, used mostly in economics, accounting and government reports. In everyday speech people simply say spending. It is usually uncountable, but the plural expenditures appears in technical writing. Typical collocations include public expenditure, capital expenditure and cut or reduce expenditure. It is often paired with income: income and expenditure. Do not confuse it with expense, which is a single cost, such as travel expenses. The verb form is expend, which is rare.
x: Household expenditure on food rose sharply during the winter months.
The council plans to cut expenditure on road repairs this year.
Her monthly income barely covers her expenditure on rent and bills.

fundraising.n: Fundraising is the uncountable noun for organised efforts to collect money, usually for a charity, school, club or political campaign. It can also be used before another noun: a fundraising dinner, a fundraising target, a fundraising manager. Businesses and start-ups also use it to mean seeking investment from backers. The related verb is raise funds, and a person who does it is a fundraiser. Remember it is one word, without a hyphen, in modern usage. Stress falls on the first syllable.
x: Our school is holding a fundraising night to buy new library books.
Online fundraising has made it easier for small charities to reach donors.
The start-up spent six months on fundraising before it found an investor.

geyser.n: A geyser is a hot spring that sends a column of water and steam into the air at intervals, as at Yellowstone or in Iceland, where the word comes from. In British English it is pronounced GEE-zer, but in American English it is often GY-zer. There is also a British sense: a gas water heater in a bathroom. Learners often confuse it with the unrelated word geezer, an informal British term for a man. Typical verbs are erupt and spout.
x: Tourists gathered around the geyser and cheered as it shot water skyward.
Iceland is famous for its geysers and hot springs.
Old Faithful is probably the best known geyser in the United States.

granite.n: Granite is a hard igneous rock made of visible crystals, widely used for kitchen worktops, monuments, paving and buildings. It is uncountable when you mean the material: a block of granite, granite worktops. Because it is so hard and lasting, it is also used figuratively: a granite jaw, or granite determination. Do not confuse it with marble, which is softer and often used for sculpture. Pronounce it GRAN-it, with the stress on the first syllable and a short final vowel.
x: The old bridge is built entirely from local granite.
They chose a black granite worktop because it resists scratches and heat.
Aberdeen is nicknamed the Granite City for its grey buildings.

implement.n: As a verb, implement means to put a plan, decision, system or law into practice. It is formal and common in business, government and IT: implement a policy, implement changes, implement a strategy. The verb is stressed on the first syllable and the last vowel is pronounced fully, while the noun, meaning a tool such as a farm implement, is almost the same word. Use it when something already decided is carried out, not when you are still deciding. The noun form is implementation.
x: The company will implement the new safety rules from January.
It took the team months to implement the software upgrade.
Several countries have failed to implement the agreement fully.

in response to.n: In response to is a preposition phrase meaning as a reaction or answer to something that has already happened or been said. It is common in news, business emails and formal writing: in response to your letter, in response to the crisis, in response to public pressure. The next word is a noun or a noun phrase, never a full clause. Do not say in response of or in response at. A shorter, more casual alternative is in reply to, which is used mainly for messages and questions.
x: In response to your email, I have attached the updated contract.
The airline added extra flights in response to the sudden rise in demand.
In response to the protests, the mayor cancelled the new parking charges.

insulating.n: Insulating is an adjective, formed from the verb insulate, that describes something which stops heat, cold, sound or electricity passing through. It often appears before a noun: insulating material, insulating layer, insulating tape, insulating foam. Do not confuse it with isolating, which means separating something or someone, although both come from the same Latin root. Wool, foam and double glazing are all good insulating materials. The noun is insulation, and the person or product is an insulator.
x: A thick insulating layer keeps the loft warm through the winter.
Electricians wrap the exposed wire with insulating tape.
Fresh snow is surprisingly insulating, which is why animals burrow into it.

itinerary.n: An itinerary is a detailed plan of a trip, listing places, dates, times and transport. Travel agents send you one, and you can say a tour or a business visit has a busy itinerary. The usual verbs are plan, follow, change and draw up an itinerary. Learners often misspell it, because the middle is pronounced quickly: i-TIN-uh-rer-ee in American English. Do not confuse it with schedule, which can refer to any timetable, or route, which is only the path. Itinerary is a countable noun.
x: The travel agent emailed us a full itinerary for our week in Italy.
Our itinerary changed when the ferry was cancelled.
The minister's itinerary includes visits to three factories.

journal.n: A journal has two main meanings. First, a serious publication for experts, such as a scientific or medical journal, where research is published after review: publish in a journal. Second, a private notebook where you write about your daily life; keep a journal is the typical collocation, close to diary. In accounting, a journal is also a record of transactions. Do not use journal for a general news magazine, which would be a magazine or newspaper. Journalist and journalism come from the same root.
x: She keeps a journal and writes in it every night before bed.
The team submitted their study to a respected science journal.
Reading old journals helps historians understand everyday life in the past.

extinction.n: Extinction is the complete disappearance of a species, and it is uncountable. The usual collocations are become extinct, face extinction, be on the verge of extinction, drive something to extinction and mass extinction. Note the adjective is extinct, not extinctioned. The phrase in danger of extinction is common, but endangered is the usual word for species at risk. In a wider sense you can also use extinction for the end of a tradition or a way of life: the extinction of local dialects.
x: Scientists warn that thousands of species are heading towards extinction.
The dinosaurs died out in a mass extinction about sixty-six million years ago.
Conservation work has saved the tiger from extinction in some regions.

feasible.n: Feasible describes a plan or idea that can actually be done, given the time, money and resources available. It is more practical than possible: something may be possible in theory but not feasible in reality. Typical collocations are feasible solution, economically feasible, technically feasible and not financially feasible. A feasibility study checks whether a project can work before money is spent. Do not confuse it with probable, which is about likelihood. The noun is feasibility, and the stress falls on the first syllable.
x: Remote working is feasible for most office jobs these days.
Engineers found that the original design was not financially feasible.
Is it feasible to finish the whole report by Friday?

feudal.n: Feudal is an adjective about feudalism, the medieval system in which lords gave land to vassals in return for loyalty and service. You will meet it in history texts: feudal system, feudal lord, feudal society, feudal Japan. Its pronunciation is FYOO-dl, with the first syllable sounding like few. It is also used figuratively, and often critically, for very unequal or old-fashioned structures: a feudal workplace. Do not confuse it with futile, which is a different word with a different meaning.
x: Under the feudal system, most farmers could not leave their lord's land.
Feudal Japan was ruled by powerful warlords and samurai.
Critics describe the company's strict hierarchy as almost feudal.

flexible.n: Flexible describes things or people that can bend or adapt easily. Physically, it means something bends without breaking: a flexible cable. In work and plans it means open to change: flexible hours, flexible working, a flexible attitude. It is generally positive, though flexible morals would be a criticism. The opposite is rigid or inflexible. Be careful with the spelling, because the ending is -ible, not -able. Stress the first syllable: FLEK-suh-bul. The noun is flexibility, and the adverb is flexibly.
x: Our company offers flexible hours so parents can pick up their children.
A flexible plastic tube connects the pump to the tank.
You need to be flexible when you travel, because plans often change.

highlight.n: As a verb, highlight means to draw special attention to something, often a problem or a point: the study highlights the risks, highlight the key results. It also means literally marking text with a coloured pen or computer tool, so you can highlight a sentence. The word is common in reports, news and presentations, and it is stronger than mention but gentler than stress. It is often followed by the importance of, the need for or the fact that. As a noun, highlights are the best moments of a match or trip.
x: The teacher asked us to highlight the main points in yellow.
Recent floods highlight the need for better drainage in the city.
Her presentation highlighted three key areas of concern.

i reckon.n: I reckon is an informal way to give an opinion, meaning I think or I guess. It is very common in British, Australian and New Zealand English and also appears in the southern United States, but it is less natural in formal writing. It is followed by a clause, with or without that: I reckon it will rain. In questions people say Do you reckon? Do not use it for strong, certain facts, since it sounds tentative. In an essay, prefer I believe or in my view.
x: I reckon we should leave early to avoid the traffic.
I reckon it will rain by lunchtime, so take an umbrella.
Do you reckon she'll get the job? I reckon she's got a good chance.

idiom.n: An idiom is a fixed expression whose meaning cannot be understood from its separate words, such as break the ice, which means start a conversation, or it's raining cats and dogs. Idioms are very frequent in speech and make English sound natural, but using them wrongly sounds odd, so learn the whole phrase and do not change the words. In linguistics idiom can also mean the particular style of a person, place or art form: a musical idiom. The adjective is idiomatic, as in idiomatic English.
x: Kick the bucket is an idiom meaning to die, so do not translate it literally.
The teacher explained the meaning of each idiom in the short story.
Her English is fluent and full of natural idiomatic phrases.

junction.n: A junction is a place where roads, railway lines or paths meet or cross. It is the standard British word, used in directions: turn left at the next junction, a busy junction. In American English you will more often hear intersection for roads, though junction is used for motorway exits and railway stations. On British motorways, junction 12 is an exit number. Electrical engineers also use it for a joint between two conductors. Do not confuse it with function, which looks similar.
x: Turn right at the first junction and you will see the station.
Traffic builds up near the junction every morning at rush hour.
Crewe is an important railway junction for trains across the north.

landfill.n: Landfill is a site where rubbish is buried in the ground, and it is also the name of the method. It is usually uncountable: waste sent to landfill, landfill sites, landfill tax. It is common in discussions about the environment, recycling and climate, since landfill produces methane. Do not confuse it with a dump, which is a looser, informal word for any place where rubbish is left. In British English you say send waste to landfill, without an article. The stress falls on the first syllable.
x: Councils are trying to reduce how much household waste goes to landfill.
The landfill outside town will be full within ten years.
Food rotting in landfill releases methane, a powerful greenhouse gas.

implicit.n: Implicit describes something suggested or understood without being stated directly: an implicit warning, implicit criticism, implicit trust. It also means absolute, with no doubts: implicit faith in someone. The opposite is explicit. Learners often mix them up, because implicit is hidden or unspoken, while explicit is clear and stated. Common collocations are implicit assumption, implicit message and implicit in. The adverb is implicitly. Stress falls on the second syllable: im-PLIS-it.
x: There was an implicit threat in his calm and polite words.
The contract contains an implicit promise that the work will be done well.
She trusted her doctor implicitly and followed every instruction.

in stock.n: In stock means that a shop or warehouse currently has an item available to buy, and the opposite is out of stock. You will see it online as a label next to products, and shop assistants use it often: Do you have this in stock? It works with the verb be or have: it is in stock, we have it in stock. A related phrase is in stock again, meaning returned to supply. Do not confuse it with on stock, which is not standard English. Stock here means goods for sale.
x: Sorry, we don't have that model in stock, but we can order it.
Is the green jacket still in stock in a medium size?
Check the website to see whether the item is in stock near you.

inherent.n: Inherent describes a quality that belongs to something as a natural and permanent part of its character, so it cannot be removed: inherent risk, inherent weakness, inherent difficulty. It is formal and often followed by in: the dangers inherent in deep-sea diving. It is stronger than natural and more abstract than basic. The adverb is inherently, as in an inherently unstable system. Do not use it for something added later, because inherent qualities are built in from the start.
x: There are inherent dangers in climbing without a rope.
Competition is inherent in a free market economy.
The design is inherently flawed and cannot be repaired easily.

inhibit.n: Inhibit means to hold back, slow down or prevent something, especially growth, development or an action. It is formal: inhibit growth, inhibit the spread of disease, inhibit creativity. In psychology, a person who is inhibited feels unable to behave naturally, usually from shyness or fear. Do not confuse it with prohibit, which means to forbid officially, though the two look similar. A typical pattern is inhibit someone from doing something. The noun is inhibition, and the opposite word in a scientific context is stimulate.
x: Cold temperatures inhibit the growth of most bacteria.
Fear of failure can inhibit people from trying new things.
The drug inhibits an enzyme that helps the virus multiply.

institute.n: As a noun, an institute is an organisation set up for a particular purpose, such as research, education or professional training: a research institute, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. It is stressed on the first syllable, IN-stit-yoot. As a verb, institute means to introduce a system, rule or legal action: institute reforms, institute proceedings. The noun is more common for learners. Do not confuse it with institution, which is broader and can mean any large organisation, including banks, hospitals or customs.
x: The institute publishes a report on climate change every year.
She studied art at a well-known institute in Paris.
The new government decided to institute a ban on single-use plastics.

integral.n: Integral describes something that is a necessary part of a whole, so the whole would be incomplete without it: an integral part of the team, an integral component, integral to success. It is formal and usually followed by to or used before part. The stress is on the first syllable in British English, though some say in-TEG-ral. Do not confuse it with integrated, which means combined into one system. In mathematics, an integral is also a noun, linked to calculus, but learners meet the adjective far more often.
x: Feedback is an integral part of how we teach writing.
Cooperation with local people is integral to the success of the project.
The camera is integral to the phone and cannot be replaced.

interact.n: Interact means to communicate with or have an effect on other people or things. For people, it is followed by with: children interact with each other. For things, it usually means to act on each other: chemicals interact, drugs interact. It is used in work, education and technology: how users interact with a website. The related noun is interaction, and the adjective is interactive. Do not say interact each other, because the verb needs with or a plural subject. The stress is on the third syllable.
x: Customers interact with our support team through a simple chat window.
Some medicines interact badly when taken at the same time.
Young children learn language by interacting with adults every day.

interval.n: An interval is a period of time or a space between two events or points. Typical phrases are at regular intervals, at intervals of ten minutes and a short interval. In British English an interval is also the break in a theatre, concert or film, which Americans call an intermission. In music, it is the distance between two notes. Stress falls on the first syllable: IN-ter-vul. Learners often forget it is a countable noun.
x: The bus runs at fifteen-minute intervals throughout the day.
We bought ice cream during the interval of the play.
There was a long interval between her first and second novels.

intervene.n: Intervene means to step into a situation on purpose in order to influence, stop or improve it: the police intervened, the government intervened in the market. It is followed by in for a situation, or between for two sides. It is formal and often used about authorities, courts and organisations. It can also mean to occur between two events, as in an intervening period. A common pattern is intervene to stop or prevent something: intervene in a dispute. Stress falls on the third syllable: in-ter-VEEN.
x: A teacher had to intervene when the argument became physical.
Central banks sometimes intervene to stop a currency from falling.
The UN agreed to intervene in the dispute between the two countries.

labour.n: Labour is the British spelling of labor, and means work, especially hard physical work, or the workers of a country or industry: cheap labour, manual labour, skilled labour. It is mostly uncountable. In the UK, the Labour Party is capitalised. Labour also means the process of giving birth: she went into labour. Do not use it for a normal job in everyday speech, where work is more natural. In American English, spell it labor. The related verb is to labour, meaning to work hard.
x: The factory depends on cheap labour from nearby villages.
She went into labour at midnight and the baby arrived at dawn.
Building the old walls took years of hard manual labour.
